summaries.example: Imagine a game with clear rules. The symbols A, B, and C are like game pieces. If A means “the bus is here” and B means “I have my bag,” then A and B together can mean “the bus is here and I have my bag.” Parentheses help show exactly which ideas belong together. A rule might say: if the bus is here and I have my bag, then I can leave.
summaries.summary: Classical logic is a carefully designed system for studying reasoning. It begins with a formal language: an alphabet of symbols and rules for making formulas. Some symbols stand for objects, properties, or relations. Other symbols mean things such as “not,” “and,” “or,” “if,” “for all,” and “there exists.” The rules make sure each formula is put together in one clear way. The system then gives rules for making deductions. It also gives semantics, which explains how formulas receive meanings and truth values in different interpretations. An argument is valid when no interpretation makes all its premises true and its conclusion false. Two important results connect proofs with meanings. Soundness says that the deduction rules never take true premises to a false conclusion. Completeness says the rules are strong enough to prove every valid argument in this system. The entry also explains that philosophers disagree about whether classical logic is the one right logic. Some favor other systems, such as intuitionistic or paraconsistent logic, for different reasons.
key_ideas: Classical logic uses a formal language with symbols, formulas, and exact grammar rules.
Premises are the starting statements in an argument; the conclusion is what the argument tries to establish.
Connectives include not, and, or, and if-then. Quantifiers express ideas such as “for all” and “there exists.”
An argument is valid when there is no interpretation in which all its premises are true but its conclusion is false.
Soundness means that anything proved by the rules is valid. Completeness means that every valid argument can be proved by the rules.
The entry also asks whether classical logic is the only correct logic. It describes alternatives without deciding that question.
summaries.why_it_matters: Logic helps people make complicated reasoning more exact. Its symbols and rules are used in mathematics, philosophy, and computer science. Studying logic also teaches an important lesson: a proof system and the meanings given to its symbols should fit together. Classical logic is powerful, but the entry shows that people can reasonably ask whether other systems handle some kinds of reasoning better.

important_terms.definition: A careful study of when reasoning supports its conclusion.
A special language made from symbols and rules for putting symbols together.
A sentence or group of sentences used to support a conclusion.
A statement that an argument is supposed to show.
An explanation of what symbols mean and when a formula is true.
A rule-based way to build a proof.

How do parentheses help prevent confusion?

Why might someone disagree with the rule that says either a statement or its opposite must be true?

summaries.example: Suppose the premises are: “Every member of the robotics club submitted a design,” and “Maya is a member of the robotics club.” The conclusion “Maya submitted a design” can be represented using a universal quantifier and a predicate. The universal rule allows us to move from a claim about every object to the corresponding claim about a particular named object. A semantic check asks whether any interpretation could make both premises true while making the conclusion false. If none can, the argument is valid.
summaries.summary: The entry presents classical elementary, or first-order, logic as a formal framework with three connected parts. Its syntax is a recursively defined collection of strings over an alphabet. Individual constants and variables function as terms; predicate letters express properties and relations; identity is treated as a logical symbol; and connectives and quantifiers build increasingly complex formulas. The formation rules give formulas unique readability, so their main connective and structure can be identified without ambiguity. The deductive system uses introduction and elimination rules for connectives, quantifiers, and identity. It defines derivability as the existence of a finite deduction from premises to a conclusion. The semantics supplies interpretations consisting of a nonempty domain and assignments of denotations or extensions to the nonlogical vocabulary. Satisfaction is defined recursively, and semantic validity means that every model of the premises is a model of the conclusion. Soundness shows that derivability implies validity; completeness gives the converse. Thus, proof-theoretic and model-theoretic consequence coincide in this system. The resulting theory also yields compactness and Löwenheim-Skolem theorems, which are mathematically powerful but indicate limits on what first-order languages can express. Finally, the entry surveys the philosophical question of whether classical logic is uniquely correct, alongside intuitionistic, relevance, paraconsistent, modal, and higher-order approaches.
key_ideas: Classical first-order logic separates syntax, deduction, and semantics. Syntax specifies well-formed formulas; deduction specifies proofs; semantics specifies interpretations and truth conditions.
Terms may be individual constants or variables. Predicate letters express properties or relations, while identity expresses sameness.
Recursive formation rules generate formulas from atomic formulas. Unique readability ensures that a formula has one structural construction, avoiding certain parsing ambiguities.

Quantifiers require careful restrictions in proof rules. Universal introduction depends on using an arbitrary term, while existential elimination requires a temporary name that does not improperly affect the conclusion.
Validity is defined by the absence of a countermodel: there must be no interpretation with true premises and a false conclusion.

Soundness and completeness establish an exact match between derivability and validity for this classical system. Compactness and the Löwenheim-Skolem results follow from that framework, while also revealing expressive limits of first-order logic.
summaries.why_it_matters: Classical logic is more than a collection of classroom rules. It is a mathematical model of deductive consequence and a foundation for major work in mathematics, philosophy, and computer science. Its soundness and completeness results explain why formal proofs and model-theoretic counterexamples can serve as two ways of studying the same consequence relation. At the same time, its limitations raise philosophical questions about whether formal rigor, intuitive reasoning, and the structure of natural language always point to one logical system.

important_terms.definition: A recursively constructed symbolic language with a fixed alphabet and precise formation rules.
A formula built from a predicate and its terms, before connectives or quantifiers are added.
A formula formed from simpler formulas using connectives or quantifiers.
A variable occurrence controlled by a quantifier; a variable not controlled by one is free.
A proof relation showing that a conclusion follows from specified premises by stated rules.
A model-theoretic relation holding when every interpretation that satisfies the premises also satisfies the conclusion.
The property that every derivable argument is semantically valid.
The property that every semantically valid argument is derivable in the system.

What is the difference between proving an argument and showing that it has no countermodel?
Why must a term used in universal introduction be treated as arbitrary?
How do compactness and Löwenheim-Skolem results suggest that first-order languages cannot express every mathematical notion?
Does the success of classical logic show that it is the only correct logic, or only that it is a useful system?

summaries.example: A school council says: “Either the science fair is on Friday or it is on Saturday.” This sentence allows both possibilities in the formal system’s “or.” If the council also says, “It is not on Friday,” a deduction can support “It is on Saturday.” But a logician can ask a different question: Is this conclusion true in every interpretation where the two premises are true? If yes, the argument is valid. The proof rules and the meaning-based test should agree.
summaries.summary: Classical logic studies reasoning through a formal language, a deductive system, and a semantics. The formal language is generated from a fixed alphabet by recursive grammar rules. Terms name or range over objects; predicates express properties and relations; atomic formulas provide the basic statements; and connectives and quantifiers form compound formulas. The syntax is designed to avoid ambiguity. In particular, parentheses and non-overlapping symbol categories help ensure unique readability, so each formula has a determinate structure. The deductive system supplies rules for deriving conclusions from premises. It includes rules for conjunction, disjunction, implication, negation, quantification, and identity, along with restrictions that protect the intended meaning of arbitrary names and existential witnesses. The semantics interprets a language over a nonempty domain and defines when formulas are satisfied. An argument is valid when every interpretation that satisfies its premises also satisfies its conclusion. This is equivalent to saying that no counterinterpretation makes the premises true and the conclusion false. The central meta-theoretic results are soundness and completeness. Soundness guarantees that derivations preserve semantic validity; completeness guarantees that every semantically valid argument has a derivation. The entry then discusses the philosophical status of classical logic. Some regard it as uniquely correct, while others defend intuitionistic, relevance, paraconsistent, higher-order, or pluralist approaches.
key_ideas: Classical logic turns parts of ordinary reasoning into a precise formal language, though the entry notes several ways to understand the relationship between formal and natural languages.
Its grammar is recursive: atomic formulas are starting points, and more complex formulas are built with connectives and quantifiers.
Parentheses and distinct symbol categories prevent different readings of the same formula. This feature is called unique readability.
A deductive system records permitted moves from premises to conclusions. Semantics instead tests formulas across interpretations and models.
Classical logic accepts principles such as double-negation elimination and the law of excluded middle. Intuitionistic logicians reject or restrict some of these principles.
Soundness and completeness connect the two approaches: the system proves exactly the arguments that are valid under its semantics.
summaries.why_it_matters: Classical logic gives precise form to questions about consequence: what follows from what, and why? Its distinction between syntax, proof, and interpretation lets researchers study reasoning from several angles and check whether those angles agree. The framework has shaped mathematics and computer science, while its expressive limits and competing logical systems remind us that formal success does not automatically settle every philosophical question about reasoning.

important_terms.definition: A language with a fixed set of symbols and exact rules for forming acceptable expressions.
A starting statement in an argument, offered in support of the conclusion.
The statement an argument aims to establish from its premises.
A symbol such as “not,” “and,” “or,” or “if-then” that combines or changes formulas.
A symbol expressing generality, such as “for all” or “there exists.”
A way of assigning a domain and meanings to the symbols of a formal language.
A proof-based relation: the conclusion can be reached from the premises by the system’s rules.
A meaning-based relation: no interpretation makes all premises true and the conclusion false.

questions_to_think_about: Is a formal language best understood as a clearer version of ordinary language, an added tool, or a mathematical model that leaves things out?
Why might “or” in a formal language include both alternatives, even when everyday speakers sometimes suggest only one?
What can a countermodel show about an argument?
Why could a logician value a system that is mathematically elegant even if it does not capture every feature of ordinary reasoning?
What reasons might support logical pluralism, the view that more than one logic can be appropriate?
